questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]=3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{11}=0:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ a & 2b\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-4)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+c\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & c \\ 0 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3},x\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$

II. $\{{b}_{1},2{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

III. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},2{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$, any vector of ${R}^{3},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This means that $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3},x\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}({b}_{1})+{x}_{2}(2{b}_{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+(2{x}_{2}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},2{b}_{2}\}$ spans ${R}^{2}$ since any linear combination of $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},2{b}_{2}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}(2{b}_{2})
$$

- Statement III is false. The set $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},2{c}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the third vector is a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that the set is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

questions.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}$ and ${R}^{2}$, respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$

III. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

- Statement II is false. The set $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the vector ${b}_{3}$ is in ${R}^{3}$ but it is not a linear combination of  ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ as the set  $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. This means that the set does not span ${R}^{3}$ and therefore, cannot be a basis.

- Statement III is false. The set $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true".
